title: Making, Evaluating and Presenting
bigQuestion: How do you carry a plan through to a finished result, judge it honestly and show your work to others?

story.title: Six O'Clock, and the Scoring Begins
story.kicker: The dinner goes onto the table, and the hardest part of the project turns out to be telling the truth about it.
paragraphs: At 5:52 p.m. Marisol pulled the thermometer from the thickest part of the chicken thigh and read 167 °F. She wrote the number and the time on the safety page taped to the cabinet, set the pan on the counter to rest, and started the timer for fifteen minutes. The soup was already at 165 °F on the back burner. The lemon bars had been cut that morning. Her phone, propped against the flour canister, had a photo of every step since Thursday.

The soup went out at 6:04, four minutes behind the plan. The chicken went out at 6:31. The rice, which she had cooked early and held in the oven, had dried a little at the edges. Her grandmother said it was the best dinner she had ever eaten, which was kind and, Marisol knew, not a rubric score.

The next day she sat down with her spec, her cost sheet, her timeline and the rubric she had written two weeks before. Served on time: soup within five minutes, excellent; chicken within fifteen, good. Portion size: one cup of soup, six ounces of chicken, met. Safety: every temperature recorded, met. Texture: rice dry at the edges, needs work. Cost: $87.40 against an $85 budget (example), over by $2.40.

Her teacher read the sheet and asked one question. "What would you change?" Marisol had an answer ready, because she had written it the night of the dinner while it was fresh: cook the rice last, not first, and buy the chicken at the store where it was $0.30 a pound cheaper. That answer, more than the chicken, was what the capstone was for.

In this chapter you will produce your own project on schedule, document it as you go, score it honestly against the spec and the rubric, and present it to an audience. Then you will look at the careers where people do exactly this work for a living.
story.think: Marisol's grandmother said it was the best dinner ever. Why is that not enough for the evaluation, and what did the rubric catch that the compliment did not?

lessons.title: Running the Timeline
lessons.mainIdea: On the production day you follow the timeline you wrote, check the clock at every checkpoint and adjust the plan, not the safety rules, when you fall behind.
reading: It is the morning of the project. The timeline is taped beside the safety page. The first task on it is not cooking; it is a five-minute walk through the plan: read every line, confirm every ingredient is in the kitchen, every tool is staged, and the thermometer has a battery. Then wash your hands for 20 seconds, tie back your hair, and start the first task at the time written next to it, not earlier and not later.

Work from the paper, not from memory. Cross off each task as it finishes and write the actual time beside the planned one. At each *checkpoint*, stop for thirty seconds and compare. If you are ahead, do not start the next hot task early; use the time to clean or to prep the next step's ingredients. If you are behind, decide what to cut, and cut the least important thing. A garnish goes before a course; a second side dish goes before the main; nothing on the safety page ever goes.

Common day-of mistakes come from skipping the paper. A student who "knows the recipe" forgets the salt; one who starts the rice first because it is easy serves it dry; one who does not write the thermometer reading cannot prove the chicken was safe. Another common mistake is doing every task in series when the timeline planned overlaps: while the chicken roasts for 90 minutes, the beans are trimmed, the table is set and the soup is reheated. The oven does the work; you do the next task.

For a sewing project the same rules hold. The timeline says press, cut, mark, sew in order, and the checkpoints fall after cutting and after the first major seam. If the first seam is off, you find it at the checkpoint with a seam gauge and rip it while it is one seam, not after the lining is in. Keep the *seam ripper* on the table, not in the box: using it early is a sign of a careful worker, not a failed one.

words.d: the day the project is actually cooked or sewn, following the timeline
a planned moment to compare actual progress to the timeline
a small hooked blade for cutting stitches to remove a seam
doing one task while another, such as roasting, runs on its own

look.title: Behind at the 4:30 Checkpoint
look.text: The 4:30 checkpoint says: chicken in the oven, soup reheating, beans trimmed, table set. It is 4:30 and the chicken went in at 4:25, the soup is still in the fridge, the beans are untrimmed, and the table is bare. Dinner is at 6:00. The plan also had a garnish of fried shallots for the soup.
look.prompt: Decide what to cut, what to overlap and what must stay unchanged, and write the new order of tasks from 4:30 to 6:00.

check.q: You reach a checkpoint 20 minutes behind. Which is the right thing to cut first?
choices: The thermometer check on the chicken
The fried shallot garnish for the soup
The hand washing after handling raw meat
check.why: Cut the least important item. Garnish goes before a course; nothing on the safety page is ever cut.

check.q: Why write the actual time beside each planned time as you work?
choices: So the evaluation can compare plan to reality and improve the next timeline
So guests know when to arrive
check.why: Recorded times are the data for honest evaluation and for a better plan next time.

check.q: The chicken roasts for 90 minutes. What should the cook be doing during that time?
choices: Opening the oven every ten minutes to check
Overlapping tasks: trimming beans, setting the table, reheating soup
check.why: The timeline plans overlaps so that the oven's time is also the cook's time for other tasks.

lessons.title: Documenting as You Go
lessons.mainIdea: Photos, times, temperatures and short notes taken during the work are the evidence you will need to evaluate the project and present it.
reading: At the evaluation Marisol could say "the chicken reached 167 °F at 5:52" because she wrote it down at 5:52. She could show the mise en place on Thursday, the cost sheet with receipts stapled to it, the chicken going into the oven, and the plated soup. None of that could have been reconstructed the next day from memory. *Documentation* is recorded while it happens or not at all.

Keep three kinds of records. First, numbers: every thermometer reading with its time, the actual start and finish time of each task, the register total from each receipt, the finished measurements of a sewn piece. Second, photos: the staged tools, each major step, each finished component, the final plate or garment from the front and back, and any problem, such as a puckered seam or a scorched pan, exactly as it looked. Third, short notes: one line when something goes differently from the plan, written in the moment. "4:41 rice done too early, holding in oven."

Set up documentation before the work so it does not slow the work. A phone on a stand at the counter, a pencil tied to the timeline, a folder for receipts. Wash your hands after touching the phone and before touching food again, and keep the phone off the prep surface; it is one of the dirtiest objects in the room. Take the photo, then wash, then continue.

Photograph problems as carefully as successes. The judge will believe a report that shows the dry rice more than one that shows only the good plates, and the dry rice is the part you learn from. A sewing student who photographs the first crooked seam beside the ripped and resewn one has shown more skill than one who shows only the finished bag.

words.d: the numbers, photos and notes recorded during a project as evidence of what happened
the store's printed record of what you bought and paid, kept for the cost sheet
records that prove a claim, such as a written thermometer reading with its time

look.title: What Would You Have Recorded?
look.text: A student's project report says: "The chicken was cooked all the way. The dinner was mostly on time. I spent about what I planned. The lemon bars were great and everyone liked them." There are two photos, both of the finished table.
look.prompt: For each sentence, name the number, photo or note that would turn it into evidence, and say when during the day it had to be taken.

check.q: Which record proves the chicken was safe to serve?
choices: A written thermometer reading of 165 °F or higher with the time it was taken
A photo of the browned skin
check.why: Only an internal temperature reading is evidence of safety; color and time are not.

check.q: Why should the phone stay off the prep surface and hands be washed after using it?
choices: Phones carry many bacteria and can contaminate food and surfaces
The teacher does not allow phones
check.why: A phone is handled constantly and is one of the dirtiest objects in a kitchen, so it is treated like any other contaminated item.

check.q: Why photograph a problem such as a scorched pan or a puckered seam?
choices: To prove the project was hard
So the evaluation is honest and the problem can be analyzed and fixed next time
Because the rubric requires ten photos
check.why: Problems are the part you learn from, and a report that shows them earns more trust than one that hides them.

lessons.title: Serving and Finishing
lessons.mainIdea: The final steps of plating and serving, or pressing and finishing, decide how the work is received, and they follow rules of temperature, timing and care like every earlier step.
reading: Twelve bowls of soup do not fill themselves. Marisol laid out twelve warmed bowls on the counter in a grid, ladled one level cup into each, wiped each rim with a clean towel, and carried them out three at a time. Hot food is served hot: above 140 °F, out of the danger zone, on warm plates. Cold food is served cold, at or below 40 °F, so the salad stayed in the refrigerator until the moment it went out. Serving is the last cooking step, and it has the same rules.

Plate in an order. The main item goes down first, in the same spot on every plate; sides go beside it; sauce goes over or under, never dripped across the rim; garnish goes on last and only if it is edible and belongs to the dish. Wipe the rim. Check every plate against the spec's portion before it leaves the counter: a scale or a measuring cup at the plating station keeps six ounces from becoming four on the last plate. Serve everyone at a table at the same time, then clear the course before the next one comes.

For a sewn piece, finishing is pressing, trimming and checking. Every seam is pressed as sewn, then open or to one side as the pattern says. Threads are clipped. Notions are tested: the snap closes, the zipper runs, the buttons hold. The piece is measured against the spec's finished measurements, and any marking chalk is brushed away. A garment is tried on the person it was made for, and the fit is noted for the evaluation.

Cleanup is part of finishing, not something after it. Leftovers go into shallow containers, labeled with the date, and into the refrigerator within two hours of cooking. The stove, boards and counters are washed and sanitized, the thermometer is wiped and put back, and the machine is covered and the iron unplugged. The rubric has a row for this, and it is the row most often lost by a project that was otherwise excellent.

words.d: arranging food on a plate in a set order and checking portion and rim before serving
hot food kept above 140 °F and cold food at or below 40 °F until served
an edible addition placed on a finished dish for appearance and flavor
the dimensions of a completed sewn piece, compared to the spec

look.title: Holding and Serving Figures
rows: cold food held at or below
look.cite: USDA and FDA food-safety guidance, standard figures
look.prompt: Marisol's rice came out of the pot at 4:41 and dinner was at 6:00. Using these rows, explain how it should have been held and what the alternative was.

check.q: Soup finished at 5:30 must be served at 6:15. How should it be held?
choices: In the pot on the counter with the lid on
Above 140 °F on a low burner or in a warm oven
In the refrigerator, then served as is
On the table so it cools to eating temperature
check.why: Hot food is held above 140 °F, above the danger zone, until it is served.

check.q: The dinner ends at 8:30 and the chicken came out of the oven at 5:52. What happens to the leftovers?
choices: Leave them on the counter to cool overnight
They were out more than two hours and must be discarded
check.why: The two-hour rule counts from when the food came out of the oven. Food out longer than two hours is thrown away.

check.q: Which is the correct order for plating?
choices: Sauce on the rim, then main
Sides first, then main on top
Main in the same spot on every plate, sides beside, sauce, garnish last, wipe the rim
check.why: A set order gives every plate the same look, and the rim wipe is the last step before the plate leaves the counter.

lessons.title: Scoring Against the Spec
lessons.mainIdea: Evaluation means putting the finished result beside the spec and the rubric line by line and recording what met, what did not and by how much.
reading: Lay the spec on the left and your documentation on the right. Read the first line of the spec: "Serves 12." Did it? Twelve bowls, twelve plates, twelve desserts: met. Next line: "Soup, 1 cup each." The ladle was a one-cup ladle and each bowl got one level scoop: met. Next: "Chicken, 6 oz each." The scale at the plating station read between 5.5 and 6.5 oz: met within a reasonable range. Go line by line to the end, and write met, not met or partly met beside each.

Then open the rubric and score each row using the evidence, not your feelings. "Served on time" is scored from the actual times written on the timeline. "Safety" is scored from the recorded temperatures. "Cost within budget" is scored from the receipts against the budget line. "Texture and doneness" is scored from tasting notes and photos, and here you must be the harshest taster at the table: the rice was dry at the edges, and dry is a texture fault, so the row is needs work even though nobody complained.

For a sewn piece, score with tools. A seam gauge on every seam; a tape measure on the finished dimensions; a close look at the stitching on both sides under good light; the closure tested ten times. Compare to the rubric levels you wrote, which used numbers such as 5/8 inch within 1/16, so there is no argument about what excellent means.

Total the weighted score and write it down before you talk to anyone. Then compare with your teacher's scoring of the same table. Where the two scores agree, you have learned to see your own work clearly. Where they differ, ask why, and look at the evidence together. Honest self-evaluation is the skill employers describe when they say someone "takes feedback well."

words.d: judging a finished result against the spec and the rubric using evidence
scoring your own work honestly before anyone else does
a small ruler with a slider used to check seam allowance and hem depth

look.title: Marisol's Rubric Scores (example, out of 4)
look.prompt: Multiply each score by its weight, total the points, and compute the maximum possible. Which two rows cost the most points, and which one was fully in Marisol's control?

check.q: The spec says 6 oz of chicken per person. How is this line evaluated?
choices: By asking guests whether they were full
By checking the recipe's serving count
By the scale readings taken at the plating station
By the weight of the raw chicken
check.why: A measurable spec line is checked with the tool named, and the plating-station scale readings are the evidence.

check.q: Nobody complained about the dry rice. How should the texture row be scored?
choices: Good, because it was only the edges
Not scored, because it was a side dish
Needs work, because dry rice is a texture fault the evidence shows
check.why: Rows are scored from evidence against the rubric's own levels, not from compliments.

check.q: Why score your own project before hearing the teacher's score?
choices: To learn to see your own work clearly and then compare where the two differ
To argue for a higher grade
Because the teacher does not score it
check.why: Self-evaluation is a skill. Comparing two independent scores shows where your judgment is accurate and where it is not.

lessons.title: Cost and Time, Plan Against Actual
lessons.mainIdea: Compare the planned cost sheet and timeline with what really happened, find every difference and name its cause.
reading: Marisol's cost sheet planned $85.00 and the receipts totaled $87.40 (example). Two dollars and forty cents over is small, but the useful question is not how much; it is where. She laid the receipts beside the sheet. Chicken: planned $2.49 per lb, paid $2.79, because the sale had ended; on 4.5 lb that was $1.35 more. Lemons: planned 6 at $0.50, bought 8 because two were soft, $1.00 more. Foil: not on the sheet at all, $0.05 short of her cushion covering it. The total told her she was over; the lines told her why.

Do the same with time. Beside each planned time on the timeline is the actual time you wrote on the day. Subtract. The soup went out 4 minutes late because the bowls were not warmed until 5:55. The chicken went out 16 minutes late because the rest ran long while the soup was cleared. The rice was done 79 minutes early because it was started first. Each *variance* has a cause, and the cause is what gets fixed next time.

Sort the causes into three kinds. Things outside your control, such as a sale that ended: you cannot prevent them, but you can plan for them with a cushion, which is exactly what the cushion is for. Things in the plan, such as starting the rice first: the plan was wrong and is rewritten. Things in the execution, such as forgetting to warm the bowls: the plan was right and was not followed, so the fix is a line on the timeline or a checkpoint that catches it.

Write the comparison as a short table with four columns: item, planned, actual, cause. Keep it to the lines that differed. Then write one sentence for money and one for time: "Over budget by $2.40 (example), mostly from the chicken price; covered by the cushion. Main course 16 minutes late, from an unplanned overlap between the rest and clearing." Those two sentences, backed by the table, are the core of the presentation.

words.d: the difference between a planned figure and the actual one, in money or time
the reason a variance happened: outside your control, a planning error or an execution error
what really happened, as recorded on the day, compared to what was planned

look.title: Planned Against Actual, Money (example)
look.prompt: Confirm the actual total from the planned total and the four changes, then sort each change into outside your control, a planning error or an execution error.

check.q: Chicken was planned at $2.49 per lb and cost $2.79 (example). For 4.5 lb, what is the variance?
check.why: The difference is $0.30 per lb, and $0.30 × 4.5 lb = $1.35.

check.q: The bowls were not warmed because the cook forgot, though the plan listed it. What kind of cause is this?
choices: An execution error, fixed with a checkpoint or a line on the timeline
check.why: The plan was right and was not followed. The fix is in how the plan is run, not in the plan itself.

check.q: What is the cushion on the cost sheet for?
choices: Buying a treat when the project is done
Rounding the total to a whole dollar
Covering price rises and forgotten items that are outside your control
check.why: The cushion exists so that a sale ending or a forgotten roll of foil does not break the budget.

lessons.title: What I Would Change
lessons.mainIdea: The most valuable page of the evaluation is a short, specific list of what you would do differently, each tied to a cause you found in the evidence.
reading: "What would you change?" is the question every judge, employer and teacher asks, and the weak answer is "nothing" or "everything." The strong answer is three to five specific changes, each tied to a variance and a cause. Marisol's list: cook the rice last and hold the chicken instead, because rice dries when held and chicken keeps in its resting period. Warm the bowls at the 5:30 checkpoint, written on the timeline. Buy chicken at the second store, $0.30 per lb cheaper. Put foil on every cost sheet. Add a two-person rule for clearing a course while the next one rests.

Each change has the same shape: the action, then the reason, then the evidence. Write it that way. "Start the rice at 5:25 instead of 3:20, because rice held for 79 minutes dried at the edges; see photo 14 and the texture row." A reader can check every part. A change without a reason is a guess; a change without evidence is an opinion.

Include what you would keep, too. The thermometer readings, the staged tools, the day-before dessert all worked, and a *reflection* that names the parts of the plan that held up is more useful than one that only lists faults. Then look for the change that would have prevented the most points lost. On Marisol's sheet that was the rice, which cost two points on a weight-2 row; the chicken price cost one point on the cost row. Fix the biggest one first.

Finally, write one sentence about the skill, not the dish: "I learned that holding time is part of the recipe." This is the sentence that transfers to the next project, to a job in a restaurant kitchen, to a garment shop, or to planning a family's week. The chicken is eaten; the sentence stays.

words.d: a written, honest look back at the project that names what worked, what did not and why
something learned on one project that applies to different work later
how long a finished food waits between cooking and serving

look.title: Turn Complaints Into Changes
look.text: A student's reflection reads: "The seams were kind of crooked. The bag took way longer than I thought. I ran out of thread. I should have been more careful." The documentation shows the first seam sewn without the seam guide taped on, the timeline with cutting taking 55 minutes against 20 planned, and a receipt for one spool of thread where the envelope listed two.
look.prompt: Rewrite the reflection as three changes, each with an action, a reason and the piece of evidence it comes from.

check.q: Which is the strongest answer to "What would you change?"
choices: Start the rice at 5:25 instead of 3:20, because holding it 79 minutes dried it; see the texture row and photo 14
check.why: A strong change names an action, a reason and the evidence, so a reader can check every part.

check.q: Why include what you would keep in a reflection?
choices: Because naming what worked tells you what to protect in the next plan
check.why: A reflection guides the next project; knowing which parts of the plan held up is as useful as knowing which failed.

check.q: Two changes are possible: fix the rice, which cost 4 weighted points, or fix the chicken price, which cost 2. Which is addressed first?
choices: The chicken price, because money matters most
The rice, because it cost the most points
check.why: Fix the change that would have prevented the most lost points first.

lessons.title: Presenting to an Audience
lessons.mainIdea: A project presentation walks the audience from the spec to the result to the changes in a set order, with evidence on every slide or page and the product itself in the room.
reading: Marisol's presentation was eight minutes long and had a shape. First, the spec: who the dinner was for and what it promised, one slide. Second, the plan: the menu, the cost sheet total and the timeline in one picture. Third, the production: six photos in order, from staged tools to the plated soup, with the thermometer reading on the chicken photo. Fourth, the evaluation: the rubric with her scores and her teacher's side by side. Fifth, the changes, three of them. Sixth, the lemon bars, on a tray, for the audience.

Bring the product when you can. A sewn piece is worn or held up and passed around; a dish is tasted, or shown on a plate if it cannot be. If the audience cannot taste, the photos must do the work, so use the plated photo taken in good light from above, not the one taken at the table under a yellow lamp. If someone in the audience has an allergy, say what is in the food before it is passed.

Speak from the evidence. "The chicken reached 167 °F at 5:52" is a stronger sentence than "I made sure it was cooked." "I was $2.40 over on an $85 budget (example), and here is where" is stronger than "I stayed pretty close to budget." Show the dry rice photo and say what you would change. An audience trusts a presenter who names the fault before they can find it.

Practice out loud twice, with a timer. Stand, look at the audience, and keep your hands off the slides. Expect questions, and have the cost sheet, timeline and safety page on the table to answer them. The two questions you will almost always be asked are "What was the hardest part?" and "What would you change?" You have already written both answers.

words.d: a spoken, ordered account of a project with evidence, given to an audience
the people you are presenting to, whose needs shape what you show and say
a slide, photo, table or object shown to support what you are saying

look.title: Reorder the Presentation
look.text: A student's slides are in this order: (1) final photo of the bag; (2) careers in fashion; (3) what I would change; (4) the cost sheet; (5) a photo of the crooked first seam; (6) the spec; (7) the rubric scores; (8) thank you. The bag itself is in a backpack under the desk.
look.prompt: Put the slides in the order this lesson teaches, cut any that do not belong, and say what should happen with the bag.

check.q: Which sentence belongs in a presentation?
choices: I was really careful about food safety
The chicken reached 167 °F at 5:52, recorded on the safety page
I think it was cooked enough
check.why: Presenters speak from evidence: a recorded temperature and time, not a feeling.

check.q: What is the first thing an audience should see in a project presentation?
choices: The spec: who the project was for and what it promised
check.why: The presentation follows the project's own order, and everything is judged against the spec, so the spec comes first.

check.q: Food will be passed to the audience. What must the presenter do first?
choices: Say what is in it so anyone with an allergy can decline
Pass it during the careers slide
check.why: Allergens are a safety matter for any audience, and naming the ingredients before passing food protects everyone.

lessons.title: Careers in Food and Nutrition
lessons.mainIdea: Culinary and dietetics careers use exactly the planning, costing, safety and evaluation skills of the capstone, at every level of education.
reading: Everything Marisol did for twelve people, a restaurant kitchen does for two hundred a night. A *sous chef* writes the prep list and the timeline; a purchasing manager keeps the cost sheet; a line cook holds the sauté station and reads the thermometer; a kitchen manager posts the safety page and checks the walk-in cooler is at or below 40 °F. Culinary careers range from a first job as a prep cook, often with no degree required, to executive chef, caterer, food stylist, recipe developer or restaurant owner.

Food safety itself is a career. Health inspectors visit restaurants and school cafeterias, check holding temperatures and hand-washing sinks, and write reports. Quality-assurance technicians in food plants test products and records. Many kitchen jobs require a food handler certificate, and managers often hold a food protection manager certification; both cover the same danger zone, temperatures and cross-contamination rules you posted on your safety page.

Dietetics is the science side. A registered dietitian nutritionist plans menus for hospitals, nursing homes, schools and sports teams, counsels people with diabetes or food allergies, and manages large food-service operations; the credential requires a degree, supervised practice and an exam. Dietetic technicians and nutrition assistants work alongside them. School nutrition directors plan meals for thousands of students under federal rules while meeting a budget, which is a cost sheet with more zeros.

Whatever the title, the interview questions will sound familiar. Tell me about a time you planned something under a deadline. How do you handle being over budget? What did you do when something went wrong? Your capstone is the answer: the spec, the cost sheet, the recorded temperatures, the dry rice and what you changed. Keep the documentation; it is your first portfolio.

words.d: the second-in-command in a kitchen, who runs prep lists, schedules and the line
a credentialed nutrition professional who plans menus and counsels people on food and health
a basic food-safety credential many kitchen jobs require
a collection of documented work you can show an employer or a school

look.title: Match the Task to the Job
look.text: Tasks from the capstone: writing the timeline; keeping the cost sheet; reading the thermometer and posting the temperature chart; planning a menu for a guest with a shellfish allergy; scoring the rubric. Jobs: sous chef, purchasing manager, health inspector, registered dietitian nutritionist, kitchen manager.
look.prompt: Match each task to the job that does it every day, and name one task that belongs to more than one job.

check.q: Which career plans menus for a hospital and counsels patients with diabetes?
check.why: Dietitians hold a credential based on a degree, supervised practice and an exam, and work in clinical and food-service nutrition.

check.q: A health inspector checks a restaurant's walk-in cooler. What reading passes?
check.why: Refrigeration must hold food at or below 40 °F, the bottom of the danger zone.

check.q: Why keep the capstone documentation after the course ends?
choices: In case the dinner is repeated
It is a portfolio that answers interview questions with evidence
check.why: Employers ask about planning, budgets and problems; the documented capstone shows all three.

lessons.title: Careers in Apparel, Children and Families
lessons.mainIdea: Apparel, early childhood, family services and consumer affairs careers each grow from one strand of the FCS course and use its planning and evaluation habits.
reading: The student who sewed the tote bag from a spec did in miniature what an apparel industry does at scale. A *patternmaker* turns a designer's sketch into the pattern pieces with grainlines and notches; a technical designer writes the spec sheet with every finished measurement and seam finish; a sample sewer makes the first one; a quality inspector measures it against the spec with a tape and a seam gauge. Related jobs include tailor, alterations specialist, costume technician for theater, textile buyer and merchandiser, and the sustainability roles now growing as companies try to cut textile waste.

Early childhood careers build on the child development strand. Preschool and child-care teachers plan a day around routines, choices and redirection; Head Start and early-intervention staff work with families of children with disabilities; a child-care center director manages safety plans, ratios, budgets and menus all at once. Most states require training hours and a background check for child-care work, and many roles require an associate or bachelor's degree. The safe-sleep rules and choking-hazard lists from your course are posted in every infant room.

Family and community services and consumer affairs are the strand that helps households manage. Family support workers, case managers and Extension educators teach budgeting, meal planning and parenting in community settings; the University of Illinois Extension runs nutrition and family programs across the state. Consumer affairs roles include credit counselors, housing counselors, and staff at agencies that handle complaints and scams. Financial literacy teachers and FCS teachers themselves are in this group, and there is a shortage of them in many districts.

Look across all of these and notice what repeats: a plan written before the work, a cost sheet, a safety page, evidence gathered as you go, an honest evaluation and a clear report. That is the capstone, and it is also a description of nearly any job worth having. Choose a strand that interests you, find one person who works in it, and ask them the question you have learned to answer: what would you change?

words.d: the apparel worker who turns a design into pattern pieces with grainlines, notches and seam allowances
services for infants and toddlers with developmental delays or disabilities and their families
a university-based teacher who brings nutrition, family and money programs to communities
work that protects and informs buyers: complaints, credit and housing counseling, scam prevention

look.title: One Skill, Five Jobs
look.text: The capstone skill: write a measurable spec and then evaluate the result against it. Five workplaces: a garment factory's quality station; an infant room at a child-care center; a credit counseling office; a school cafeteria kitchen; a theater costume shop.
look.prompt: For each workplace, describe what the spec would contain and what tool or record would be used to check the result against it.

check.q: Which job writes the spec sheet with every finished measurement and seam finish for a garment?
check.why: The technical designer's spec sheet is the industry version of the capstone specification.

check.q: Which rule from the child development strand is posted in every licensed infant room?
choices: Infants sleep on their stomach to prevent spit-up
Infants sleep on their back on a firm, flat surface with nothing else in the crib
Infants sleep with a soft blanket for warmth
Infants nap in a car seat
check.why: Safe sleep is on the back, on a firm flat surface, with nothing else in the crib.

check.q: What does nearly every FCS career have in common with the capstone?
choices: A college degree in the same subject
A plan, a cost sheet, a safety rule set, evidence, evaluation and a report
check.why: The capstone's cycle of plan, cost, produce, document, evaluate and present is the shape of the work in every strand.

review.q: At a checkpoint you are 20 minutes behind. Which may never be cut to catch up?
choices: The thermometer reading on the chicken
review.why: Nothing on the safety page is ever cut; garnishes and extras go first.

review.q: Which is evidence that a dish met the safety plan?
choices: A written internal temperature with the time it was read
A photo of the browned crust
A guest saying it tasted done
review.why: Only a recorded thermometer reading proves the safe minimum internal temperature was reached.

review.q: Hot soup must wait 45 minutes before serving. What temperature must it be held above?
review.why: Hot food is held above 140 °F, the top of the danger zone, until served.

review.q: A cost sheet planned $85 and receipts total $87.40 (example). What is the most useful next step?
choices: Compare line by line to find which items caused the variance and why
review.why: The lines, not the total, show the causes, and the causes are what get fixed next time.

review.q: The plan listed warming the bowls and the cook forgot. What kind of cause is this?
review.why: The plan was right and was not followed; the fix is a checkpoint or a timeline line that catches it.

review.q: Which is the strongest "what I would change" statement?
choices: Start the rice at 5:25, because holding it 79 minutes dried it, as photo 14 and the texture row show
review.why: Action, reason and evidence together make a change a reader can check.

review.q: In what order should a project presentation run?
choices: Spec, plan, production, evaluation, changes, product
Product, then whatever the audience asks
review.why: The presentation follows the project's own order, from the spec everything is judged against to the finished product.

review.q: Which credential plans hospital menus and counsels patients on nutrition?
review.why: The registered dietitian nutritionist credential requires a degree, supervised practice and an exam.
